catalog_quote: En otomí todas las palabras se acentúan prosódicamente en el mismo lugar y por lo tanto no es necesario escribir el acento. La sílaba con la acentuación principal es siempre la primera sílaba del radical. Las partículas que se anteponen al verbo, al sustantivo y al adjetivo, aunque escritas como palabras independientes, no se acentúan.¹¹ Son sólo las palabras con significado propio las que se acentúan. En las palabras de más de dos sílabas y las palabras compuestas, se acentúa cada tercer sílaba, es decir una sí y otra no, para satisfacer el patrón rítmico, del que se hablará más adelante. Ejemplos: ra fani la bestia / hont'a nada más / ra t'axahua la trucha / ra do'yo'bofani el caballo negro y flaco [stressed syllables underlined in the original: fa, høn, t'a + hua, do + bo + ni] (p. 23) ... Hay que tener mucho cuidado de no confundir el tono con el acento. El acento no se escribe en otomí. (p. 24) ... Además de tonal, el otomí es rítmico.¹³ Tanto la fonología o sistema de sonidos, como la gramática se alteran a fin de lograr el patrón rítmico del idioma, que tiende a agrupar las sílabas por pares.¹⁴ De cada par, la primera se acentúa y la segunda no. (p. 25) ... el patrón rítmico del idioma, que requiere que la primera y tercera sílabas del radical sean las acentuadas. (p. 50) ... 11. Se escriben aparte, como si fueran palabras independientes, para hacer destacar la sílaba inicial de la raíz, que es siempre la acentuada. (note 11)
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: En otomí todas las palabras se acentúan prosódicamente en el mismo lugar y por lo tanto no es necesario escribir el acento. La sílaba con la acentuación principal es siempre la primera sílaba del radical. Las partículas que se anteponen al verbo, al sustantivo y al adjetivo, aunque escritas como palabras independientes, no se acentúan. Son sólo las palabras con significado propio las que se acentúan. En las palabras de más de dos sílabas y las palabras compuestas, se acentúa cada tercer sílaba, es decir una sí y otra no, para satisfacer el patrón rítmico [...] (p. 25:) [el idioma] tiende a agrupar las sílabas por pares. De cada par, la primera se acentúa y la segunda no.
new_statements.translation: In Otomi all words are prosodically stressed in the same place and therefore it is not necessary to write the accent. The syllable with the main stress is always the first syllable of the radical (stem). The particles placed before the verb, noun and adjective, although written as independent words, are not stressed. Only words with meaning of their own (content words) are stressed. In words of more than two syllables and in compound words, every other syllable is stressed ('one yes, the next no') to satisfy the rhythmic pattern [...] (p. 25:) [the language] tends to group syllables in pairs. Of each pair, the first is stressed and the second is not.
new_statements.citation: Echegoyen Gleason, Artemisa. 1979. Luces contemporáneas del otomí: gramática del otomí de la sierra. México: Instituto Lingüístico de Verano.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File checked: (357-leaf Rosetta Project scan, archive.org rosettaproject_otm_book-1) plus the IA text. I rendered PDF leaf 18 (printed p. 23, running head 'EL ACENTO') and leaf 20 (p. 25, 'EL RITMO') and read them as images. The quoted passage is on p. 23 under 'C. Otras Observaciones sobre la Escritura y Pronunciacion del Otomi, 1. El Acento' word for word: 'En otomi todas las palabras se acentuan prosodicamente en el mismo lugar y por lo tanto no es necesario escribir el acento. La silaba con la acentuacion principal es siempre la primera silaba del radical. Las particulas que se anteponen al verbo, al sustantivo y al adjetivo, aunque escritas como palabras independientes, no se acentuan.…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress is fixed on the first syllable of the radical (root/stem) of content words; preposed grammatical particles (proclitics for TAM/person, articles etc.) are unstressed and outside the stress domain; suffixes follow the stem. The language is also tonal (high, low, falling, rising per syllable), and the authors explicitly distinguish tone from stress; stress is not.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Rhythmic alternating stress: syllables are grouped in pairs (trochaic), the first of each pair stressed; in words of more than two syllables and in compounds the 1st and 3rd syllables of the radical are stressed (p. 23, p. 25, p. 50); suffixes have mono-/disyllabic allomorphs and some disyllabic radicals apocopate to preserve the binary rhythm.
new_statements.exceptions: Proclitic particles never stressed; in compounds, syllables that become 2nd or 4th lose their original stress (p. 50); in adjective+noun compounds the adjective radical (first element) carries the main word stress (p. 67); certain stressed particles (xin 'tampoco', bin) take longer variants (xinda/xingui, hinga/hingui) before a stressed radical to avoid two adjacent stressed syllables (pp. ~250ff.). Vowel of definite articles and the reverential is not stressed (note to p. ~55).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the radical (stem) plus suffixes = the orthographic content word; proclitics are written separately precisely because they are unstressed (note 11: 'para hacer destacar la sílaba inicial de la raíz, que es siempre la acentuada'). If proclitics are counted as part of the phonological word, the reading is stem-initial (morphologically determined) rather than strictly word-initial. Tonal language with an explicit stress statement (could also be coded tone language with a stress statement). Variety: San Gregorio and San Antonio el Grande, Huehuetla, Hidalgo.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Otomí de la Sierra as spoken in San Gregorio and San Antonio el Grande, municipio Huehuetla, Hidalgo (data credited to speakers from both towns; preface signed Ixmiquilpan 1976) = Eastern Highland Otomi, east2556 / otm. This is the 1979 first edition (Echegoyen sole named author, analysis credited to Jenkins and Voigtlander); Glottolog's 1985 'Voigtlander & Echegoyen' entry is the 2nd edition of the same book. Not to be confused with Tenango Otomi (otn, tena1241), a neighbouring Sierra variety.

new_statements.translation: In Otomi all words are stressed prosodically in the same place and therefore it is not necessary to write the accent. The syllable with the main stress is always the first syllable of the root. The particles placed before the verb, the noun and the adjective, although written as independent words, are not stressed. Only words with meaning of their own are stressed. In words of more than two syllables and in compound words, every third syllable is stressed, that is, one yes and one no, to satisfy the rhythmic pattern, which will be discussed later. [p. 23] ... Besides being tonal, Otomi is rhythmic. ... the rhythmic pattern of the language, which tends to group syllables in pairs. Of each pair, the first is stressed and the second is not. [p. 25]

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (initial-syllable initial stress) and the same source as the existing statement. (ii) alternating trochaic secondary stress in longer words and compounds (pp. 23, 25, 50); (iii) adjective root carries main stress in adj+noun compounds (p. 67); (iv) the language is tonal with stress independent of tone (p. 24). quote re-verified on the page scan of leaves 18 and 20.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Main stress always on the first syllable of the root (radical); proclitic particles written as separate words (articles, verb prefixes, etc.) are unstressed and stand outside the stress domain (note 11: they are written apart precisely 'to make the initial syllable of the root, which is always the stressed one, stand out'). The language is tonal (high, low, and falling/rising combinations, p. 24) and the author warns not to confuse tone with stress ('El acento no se escribe en otomí. El tono es el nivel musical en que se pronuncia la sílaba', p. 24).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Trochaic alternation from the root-initial syllable: in words of more than two syllables and in compounds, every other syllable (1st, 3rd..) is stressed, syllables grouped in pairs with the first of each pair stressed (pp. 23, 25; p. 50: 'requiere que la primera y tercera sílabas del radical sean las acentuadas'). Suffix allomorphs (one- vs two-syllable variants) and apocope of disyllabic roots are chosen to keep the pairing (note 14; p. 25; p. 212). In adjective+noun compounds the adjective root carries the main stress (p. 67: 'es el radical adjetivo el que lleva el acento principal de la palabra'), i.e., the first root of the compound, consistent with root-initial stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None to the placement rule as such. Unstressed items: articles ra/ya, the reverential zi, and preverbal/prenominal particles (p. 23; note on p. 39: 'La vocal en los artículos determinados y el reverencial no se acentúa'). When a root's first syllable would end up in an even (unstressed) position inside a compound it loses its original stress and some disyllabic roots undergo apocope to preserve the rhythm (p. 50; note 22 on menzeshni). Rhythmic (alternating) stress marked in examples is distinct from main stress. Dialect note 12: San Antonio lacks the falling tone; San Gregorio's rising tone is a variant of high after low (tone, not stress).
new_statements.identity_note: Echegoyen 1979 describes 'otomí de la Sierra' as spoken in the municipio of Huehuetla, Hidalgo and adjoining municipios of Hidalgo, Puebla and Veracruz, with the analysis based in particular on the speech of San Antonio el Grande and San Gregorio (Introducción, text lines 160-168); the author notes gradual transitions toward Tenango Otomi and marks a few San Antonio vs San Gregorio differences (tone inventory, note 12). This matches Glottolog east2556 (Eastern Highland Otomi, otm), so the work is about the catalog language, not another variety.

sources.note: TAM description of the yühǘ of Santa María Apipilhuasco; an inflected verb = verbal proclitic (coding TAM and person) + verb stem; four conjugation classes defined by proclitic sets (after Voigtlander & Echegoyen 1985, Palancar 2011, Hernández-Green 2015); 'la mutación consonántica y la flexión tonal del verbo' are named among the topics treated. No tone inventory or phonology chapter is visible from the record; whether the thesis has one is not seen.

sources.note: Reanalysis of Voigtlander & Echegoyen's seven conjugation classes over 2,000 verbs, reduced to five (a nasal marker reanalysed as derivational); the abstract has no tone wording. Relevance to tone is indirect: in this variety the conjugation classes are distinguished by proclitic sets whose only difference is often high vs low tone (held Gramática yuhú: 'el tono en los proclíticos verbales, es la única diferencia entre..'), so the paper necessarily handles proclitic tone as an inflectional exponent; listed last, as a morphology paper, for verification to keep or drop.
